title: Building the application package
summary: A lending package is the evidence that closes each of the four risks and answers each of the five Cs, arranged so a relationship manager can write the credit memo from it. The sources and uses table and a one-page summary carry most of the weight.
body:
The application package is not a pile of documents; it is the credit memo, written in advance, with the evidence attached. Mr Shabazz, a package arranged the way a committee reads gets a fast answer, and one that makes the relationship manager hunt gets parked.

In plain English

Everything in the earlier weeks becomes a document here. The lender wants to see who you are, what you are building, what it costs, how it is paid for, how the loan will be repaid, what protects the bank, and what could go wrong. Each answer needs evidence the bank can check, and all of it must agree with everything else.

The professional framing: what to bring to a formal application

  1. Executive summary, one page. Asset, location, program, total cost, the loan requested, the repayment source, the security offered.
  2. Sponsor profile. Curriculum vitae, personal net worth and liquidity statement, and the team page naming the contractor, cost consultant, development manager and property manager with their completed projects.
  3. Corporate documents. Incorporation of the borrowing company, its directors and shareholders, and a resolution authorising it to borrow.
  4. Title and survey. Evidence of ownership in the borrower's name and a current survey.
  5. Approvals. Written planning and building approvals, or a clear schedule for them.
  6. Appraisal. As-is land value and as-complete value, by a valuer the lender accepts.
  7. Cost evidence. An independent cost consultant's or quantity surveyor's budget, and the construction contract or tender results.
  8. Financial model. NOI built the lender's way, coverage with sensitivities, the sizing tests and a sources and uses table.
  9. Market evidence. Market study, rent comparisons, and any leases, letters of intent or pre-sale contracts.
  10. Schedules. Construction programme and monthly draw schedule.
  11. Operations. Insurance plan and property-management proposal.
  12. Evidence of equity. Bank statements, escrow letters and paid invoices.

The professional framing: sources and uses

The sources and uses table is the single most-read page after the summary. Uses lists every cost: land, hard construction cost, soft costs, contingency, financing fees and construction interest. Sources lists every dollar paying for them: the loan, cash equity, land equity and any other layer. The two columns must total the same figure, and every number must match the model, the budget and the summary.

A worked example

A hypothetical project's sources and uses, all in US dollars.

UsesAmountSourcesAmount
Land150,000Senior loan650,000
Hard construction cost650,000Cash equity, spent200,000
Soft costs90,000Land equity, credited150,000
Contingency50,000
Fees and construction interest60,000
Total1,000,000Total1,000,000

Now check it the way a reviewer would. The loan is 65 percent of total cost, matching a 65 percent loan-to-cost limit. Equity is US$350,000, 35 percent. Contingency is US$50,000, about 7.7 percent of hard cost; the reviewer will ask whether the cost consultant supports that figure. Construction interest is inside the budget. Land is credited at US$150,000; the reviewer will check whether that is cost or appraisal and whether this lender accepts it. If the model's summary said total cost was US$980,000, the whole package would lose credibility on one line.

The professional framing: writing for the memo

Write paragraphs the relationship manager can lift. Use the bank's headings: borrower, purpose, sources and uses, repayment, security, risks and mitigants. Put a risks table near the front, naming completion, lease-up, cash flow, exit, currency and sponsor risk, with the evidence that closes each. State what is unknown plainly, with the date by which it will be known. Number every page and every appendix so a question can be answered by reference.

The professional framing: the readiness gates

Before a formal application, check yourself against a short list of gates, each of which a lender will otherwise check for you. Is the borrowing company formed and authorised? Is title in its name, or the structure documented? Are approvals in writing? Is the budget prepared by an independent cost professional? Is the model rebuilt on current figures and reconciled to the budget? Is equity paid in with evidence? A package submitted with any of these open invites a conditional approval at best, and a decline at worst. A package submitted with all of them closed lets the committee spend its time on the commercial questions, which is where you want it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an inconsistency. Two documents giving different costs, a rent in the model that differs from the market study, or an equity figure that does not match the bank statements will each make a reviewer doubt every other number. Reconcile the whole package line by line before it leaves you, and keep one master version.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sends everything, unsorted, in the belief that more paper looks more serious. It does the opposite. A reviewer facing a hundred unlabelled pages concludes that the sponsor does not know what matters. Send what the bank asked for, in its order, with an index.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, build the package as a binder with an index, a one-page summary and a sources and uses table on page two, and treat every other document as an appendix that supports a sentence in the summary. Before sending, run a reconciliation: every total cost, loan amount, equity figure, rent and date across every document, listed side by side. Then ask your relationship manager what is missing for credit risk before it is formally submitted. Professional sign-off required: cost consultant for the budget, licensed valuer for the appraisal, accountant for the model and financial statements, and lawyer for corporate and title documents.

Your construction document-control habits translate directly. A package is a controlled document set: one master, a revision log, and nothing sent that has not been checked against the current revision.
checklist: Executive summary, sponsor and team, corporate documents, title, approvals, appraisal.
Independent budget, construction contract, financial model and sources and uses.
Market evidence, schedules, insurance, property management and evidence of equity.
Sources and uses must balance and match every other document.
Write in the memo's order with a risks table near the front.
Reconcile every figure across every document before sending.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Your summary states total cost of US$1,200,000; the cost consultant's budget totals US$1,250,000 because it includes construction interest; the model uses US$1,200,000. What will the reviewer conclude, and how do you fix it?
selftest.a: The reviewer will conclude that total cost is understated by about US$50,000 of construction interest and that the sponsor's numbers do not reconcile, lowering trust in the whole file. Fix it by adopting the complete figure, US$1,250,000, everywhere; rerun the sizing tests (the equity requirement rises), update the sources and uses so it balances, and resend one consistent version.

apply: Prepare a sources and uses table for a hypothetical project and check that it balances and that the loan equals the lender's loan-to-cost limit.

title: The lender-meeting playbook
summary: The first meeting with a lender is not to get a loan; it is to learn the bank's appetite and leave the relationship manager wanting to write your memo. Meetings come in a set order, with predictable questions and strict rules of conduct.
body:
You meet a lender three times in sequence: an appetite call, a pre-screen and a formal application, and each has a different purpose. Mr Shabazz, the first conversation is for learning, so arrive with questions and leave with notes, not with a request for money.

In plain English

Before a bank will look seriously at your project, you want to know whether it lends on this kind of building, in this place, at this size, and what it needs to see. That conversation is informal. Once your package is ready, you test it with a summary and ask for indicative terms. Only then do you submit a full application. Skipping straight to the application, or turning the first conversation into a sales pitch, wastes both sides' time.

The professional framing: three meetings in order

  1. Appetite call. Informal, no package. "Do you lend on this asset type, in this location, at this size? What do you need to see?" Present no figures as bankable; this is a learning conversation.
  2. Pre-screen. A summary package: a short teaser, sources and uses, sponsor profile. Ask for indicative terms in writing.
  3. Formal application. The full package from yesterday's lesson, once your own readiness gates are cleared: entity formed, title resolved, budget independent, model reconciled.

The professional framing: what they will ask, and what they are testing

  • "How much of your own cash is in?" Commitment and the first-loss cushion.
  • "Who prepared the budget?" Cost certainty.
  • "What happens if costs run 15 percent over?" Who funds the overrun, and how quickly.
  • "What if lease-up takes twice as long?" Your liquidity to carry the building.
  • "Who manages construction?" Execution risk.
  • "What is your exit if we do not convert?" The second way out.
  • "Who else are you talking to?" Competition and seriousness.

The professional framing: your questions for them

  • What are your maximum loan-to-cost and minimum coverage ratio for this asset type?
  • Do you credit land at appraisal or at cost?
  • What guarantees do you normally take, and can they burn off at completion or stabilisation?
  • Who certifies draws, and how quickly do draws pay after certification?
  • What is your approval timeline and committee cycle?
  • Do you lend in local currency, US dollars or both?

A worked example

A hypothetical sponsor plans her approach to lenders for a US$650,000 loan.

  1. Week 1: appetite calls with two banks. Bank A lends on this asset type up to 60 percent of cost with land at cost. Bank B lends up to 65 percent with land at appraisal and burns off completion guarantees at practical completion.
  2. On her figures, Bank A's terms give a loan of about US$600,000 and Bank B's about US$650,000. Bank B leads.
  3. Weeks 2 to 6: she closes the gaps both banks named: a cost consultant's budget and a signed pre-lease.
  4. Week 7: pre-screen with Bank B; indicative terms received in writing.
  5. Week 9: formal application to Bank B, with Bank A kept informed as a credible alternative.

Two focused conversations, used to fix the package before anything formal, produced a better offer than ten simultaneous applications would have.

The professional framing: rules of conduct

  • Never overstate approvals, leases or commitments.
  • Never leave figures you cannot defend.
  • Send a written summary after every meeting, recording what was said and what you will provide.
  • Get any indicative terms in writing; verbal comfort is not approval.
  • Answer hard questions directly and say "I do not know yet, and I will know by this date" when that is true.

The professional framing: reading the answers you receive

Listen for three kinds of answer in an appetite call. A firm figure, such as a maximum loan-to-cost, is credit policy and rarely moves. A range, such as "usually between this and that", signals room to negotiate for a strong file. A deflection, such as "we would need to see the numbers", often means the asset type, location or size sits at the edge of the bank's appetite. Record which kind each answer was. Two banks quoting the same headline limit can be very different prospects if one gave you a firm number and the other a deflection. Ask, too, what the bank has financed recently that resembles your project; a bank that has done one recently understands the risks and has a reference point in its own book.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is credibility lost early. A figure presented as firm in an appetite call that later changes, or an approval described as granted that is still pending, follows you into the credit memo. Lenders in a small market talk to one another, and a reputation for overstatement is very hard to repair.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner shops a weak package to every bank at once. Banks talk, and a deal seen and declined by several lenders becomes harder to place, because each new lender asks why the others said no. Approach one or two first, fix what they find, then widen the circle if needed.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, prepare a one-page answer sheet to the seven questions above before any formal meeting, and rehearse it aloud with someone playing a sceptical credit officer. Keep a lender log: date, bank, attendees, what they said about appetite and terms, what you promised and by when. Send the written summary within a day. Professional sign-off required: if any figures or investor terms are discussed, confirm with your lawyer what you may represent, and with a securities lawyer before mentioning any offering to investors.
checklist: Appetite call first: learn, do not apply.
Pre-screen with a summary; get indicative terms in writing.
Formal application only once your own readiness gates are cleared.
Prepare answers to the seven standard questions.
Ask about loan-to-cost, coverage, land credit, guarantees, draw speed, timeline and currency.
Approach one or two lenders first; never shop a weak package widely.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: In an appetite call, the relationship manager asks for your expected coverage ratio. Your model is still being rebuilt. What do you say?
selftest.a: Say plainly that the model is being rebuilt and you will not give a figure you cannot defend, describe the assumptions you are testing (rent evidence, vacancy, costs), and commit to a date when you will send the reconciled figure. Ask what minimum coverage the bank normally requires so you can test against it. Follow up in writing.

apply: Write your one-page answers to the seven standard lender questions for a hypothetical project and rehearse them aloud.

title: After the money moves: draws, reporting and conversion
summary: Closing is the start of the relationship, not the end. A construction loan is administered draw by draw, with reporting covenants, covenant tests and finally conversion or refinancing, and a borrower who reports early and accurately keeps the bank's trust when something goes wrong.
body:
Once a loan closes, the work changes from persuading the bank to administering the loan: draws, reports, covenant tests and finally conversion. Mr Shabazz, a borrower who reports early and accurately buys the goodwill that matters most when a problem arrives.

In plain English

The commitment letter and loan agreement are signed and security is registered. From now on the bank watches the project through a regular stream of documents: payment applications, cost certificates, progress reports, insurance certificates, accounts and, once the building opens, rent rolls. Each one is checked against the promises in the loan agreement. If they line up, money keeps flowing. If they do not, the bank asks questions, and eventually it can stop funding.

The professional framing: the monthly draw cycle

  1. The contractor submits a payment application for work done in the month.
  2. Your own team checks it, then sends it with a draw request to the bank.
  3. The bank's monitoring cost consultant inspects the site and certifies the work actually done.
  4. The bank runs the in-balance test on the latest cost to complete.
  5. The bank pays the certified amount, less retention, usually to the contractor.
  6. Lien waivers or equivalent confirmations are collected where required.

Agree the calendar in writing: when requests are due, how long certification takes and when payment is made. Align the construction contract's payment terms with it.

The professional framing: reporting covenants

Expect monthly progress and cost reports during construction, quarterly management accounts, annual reviewed or audited statements, annual personal financial statements from any guarantor, insurance renewals, and once the building operates, rent rolls and operating statements. Missing a reporting deadline is usually an event of default in its own right, even if everything else is fine.

The professional framing: covenant monitoring

Financial covenants are tested on set dates, often quarterly or annually. Do not wait for the bank to test them. Run your own test every month on trailing figures and a forecast for the next two test dates. A breach you foresee three months out can often be managed by a cash deposit, a temporary waiver or an amendment agreed calmly. A breach the bank discovers is an event of default.

The professional framing: conversion or refinancing

At practical completion, the bank receives occupancy permits, the final cost certificate and an as-built appraisal. The loan then waits for stabilisation: the building must reach the bank's income test, typically a coverage ratio held for a set number of months. When it does, a construction-to-permanent facility converts to an amortising term loan, or a take-out lender repays it. Plan the conversion test months in advance, because the date it is measured on decides whether your loan converts or falls due.

A worked example

A hypothetical loan of US$650,000 must convert when coverage reaches 1.20 times on three months of trailing NOI, annualised, by month 30, or the loan falls due. Amortising debt service at conversion would be about US$60,202 a year.

  1. Required annualised NOI: 1.20 times US$60,202, about US$72,242.
  2. At month 24, the building is 80 percent let. Trailing annualised NOI is US$62,000, coverage about 1.03 times.
  3. The sponsor's own forecast shows 90 percent occupancy by month 28, giving NOI of about US$71,000, still short of US$72,242.
  4. She raises it with the bank at month 24, not month 30. Options discussed: a six-month extension of the conversion date, a partial paydown of about US$11,000 so the smaller loan converts at the available NOI, or a cash reserve held against the shortfall.
  5. The bank grants a three-month extension with a fee, because the problem was raised early with a credible forecast.

The professional framing: change orders and the bank

During construction, the loan agreement usually requires the bank's consent for change orders above a set size, and for any change to the construction contract, the contractor or the schedule beyond a threshold. Treat that consent as part of your change-control procedure. A change agreed with the contractor without the bank's consent can make the next draw uncertifiable, because the cost consultant will be certifying work that is not in the approved budget. Keep a change log that shows, for each change, its cost, its effect on contingency and the cost-to-complete position, and whether bank consent was needed and obtained.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting reporting slip during the busiest part of construction, exactly when the bank most wants to see the numbers. A late report reads as either disorganisation or concealment, and a bank that cannot see the project assumes the worst.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats closing as the finish line and stops managing the bank. The relationship manager who championed the loan now has to defend it at every review. Make that easy with clean, early reports, and with bad news delivered by you before it is found by the bank.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, set up a lender compliance calendar on the day of closing: every report, every covenant test date, every insurance renewal and the conversion test date, each with an owner and a reminder two weeks ahead. Run your own covenant test monthly. Hold a short monthly call with the relationship manager during construction, with a one-page update on cost, schedule, contingency remaining and leasing. Your operations background is the right instinct here: a lender is a supervising authority, and a clear, regular status report with exceptions flagged is what keeps it from intervening. Professional sign-off required: monitoring cost consultant for certifications; accountant for covenant calculations and statements.
checklist: Agree the draw calendar in writing and align the construction contract with it.
Reporting covenants are events of default if missed.
Test your own covenants monthly, ahead of the bank.
Plan the conversion test months in advance.
Raise foreseeable problems early with a credible forecast.
Set up a compliance calendar with owners and reminders on closing day.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Six months before the conversion test, your forecast shows coverage reaching only 1.12 times against a 1.20 times requirement. What do you do, and when?
selftest.a: Act now. Tell the relationship manager in writing, with the forecast and its assumptions, and propose options: an extension of the conversion date, a partial paydown sized so the smaller loan meets 1.20 times on the forecast NOI, a cash reserve, or a temporary covenant amendment. Early notice with a credible plan is far more likely to get agreement than a breach found at the test date.

apply: Build a lender compliance calendar for a hypothetical 18-month construction loan listing every report, test date and renewal with an owner.

title: When a loan gets into trouble: waivers, amendments and workouts
summary: When a project slips toward breach, the borrower's best outcomes come from early disclosure and a credible plan: a waiver, an amendment or a negotiated workout. Enforcement is the bank's last resort and usually the worst outcome for both sides.
body:
Most troubled loans are resolved by negotiation, not enforcement, and the borrower's position is strongest before a breach, not after. Mr Shabazz, the moment you can see a covenant failing is the moment to call the bank, with numbers and a plan.

In plain English

Things go wrong on real projects: a cost overrun, a slow lease-up, a tenant failure, a rate rise. Banks expect some loans to need help. What they do not tolerate is surprise. A bank has a set of tools short of enforcement, and it will use them for a borrower it trusts, who tells it early and shows how the problem will be fixed. The same bank will move quickly to protect itself against a borrower it thinks is hiding something.

The professional framing: the ladder of responses

  1. Waiver. The bank agrees not to treat a specific breach as a default, often for a single test date, sometimes for a fee.
  2. Amendment. The bank changes a term going forward: a lower covenant for a period, a longer conversion date, a revised draw schedule.
  3. Cash cure or paydown. You deposit cash or repay part of the loan to bring a ratio back into compliance. Many loan agreements give an explicit right to cure in this way, limited in number.
  4. Forbearance or standstill. The bank agrees not to enforce for a set period while a plan is carried out, usually in exchange for tighter controls, more reporting, fees and sometimes more security.
  5. Restructuring. A wider rewrite: extended term, changed amortisation, new equity, a partial sale, or the introduction of a new investor or lender.
  6. Enforcement. The bank demands repayment and enforces its security: appointing a receiver, taking control through the share pledge, stepping into the construction contract or selling the property.

The professional framing: what the bank wants to see

An honest diagnosis of the problem, a revised forecast built the bank's way, a specific plan with dates, evidence that the sponsor is contributing, for example new equity or deferred fees, and better information flow. Banks almost always ask the sponsor to share the pain. A request that asks the bank to carry all of the extra risk is rarely accepted.

A worked example

A composite hypothetical case. A US$650,000 term loan has annual debt service of about US$60,202 and a 1.20 times covenant tested annually. A major tenant leaves, and NOI falls from US$80,000 to US$70,000.

  1. Coverage becomes US$70,000 divided by US$60,202, about 1.16 times. The next test is in four months.
  2. To meet 1.20 times on NOI of US$70,000, debt service can be at most US$70,000 divided by 1.20, about US$58,333. At the same rate and amortisation that supports a loan of about US$629,800. A paydown of about US$20,200 would restore compliance.
  3. The sponsor calls the bank now, presents the numbers, and proposes three things: a US$20,000 paydown from her own funds, a signed letter of intent from a replacement tenant at a similar rent starting in six months, and monthly leasing reports until the space is let.
  4. The bank accepts, with a small amendment fee, and agrees a temporary reporting covenant. No default is recorded.
  5. Had the sponsor waited for the bank's test, the same figures would have produced an event of default, a reservation of rights letter, legal costs, a default interest rate and a much weaker negotiating position.

The professional framing: the reservation of rights letter

When a bank learns of a breach it has not yet decided how to treat, it often sends a reservation of rights letter. The letter says the bank knows of the default and is not giving up any of its remedies by continuing to deal with you. It is not enforcement, but it is a serious signal: from that point the bank can act without further warning, and its patience is no longer implied by its silence. Respond to such a letter promptly, in writing, with your lawyer's input, setting out the facts and your proposed plan. Do not treat continued funding after such a letter as forgiveness.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that a default triggers cross-default or guarantee calls elsewhere. Many loan agreements and guarantees say that a default on one loan is a default on others, and a guarantor's liquidity covenant may be breached at the same time. A single missed test can cascade across your affairs. Read the cross-default clauses before you sign and again when trouble appears.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner goes quiet, hoping the problem resolves before the next test. Silence is the most expensive choice available. It turns a negotiable problem into an event of default, and it destroys the trust that a waiver or amendment depends on. The second mistake is making a payment to an unsecured creditor or an investor while the bank loan is in breach, which may itself breach a negative covenant.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, keep a simple early-warning sheet: contingency remaining, cost-to-complete position, leasing against plan, and coverage and loan-to-value against covenant at the next two test dates. Set a trigger, such as coverage within 0.10 of the covenant, that means you call the bank that week. When you do, bring the diagnosis, the revised forecast, your own contribution and a dated plan. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer acting only for you before signing any waiver, amendment, forbearance or restructuring, and an insolvency adviser if the borrowing company may not be able to pay its debts as they fall due, because directors can have personal duties at that point [unverified — confirm the law in the jurisdiction].
checklist: Disclose early, with numbers and a plan, before a breach is tested.
Responses short of enforcement: waiver, amendment, cash cure, forbearance, restructuring.
Banks expect the sponsor to share the pain, for example with new equity.
A paydown can be sized from NOI divided by the covenant ratio.
Default can cascade through cross-default clauses and guarantor covenants.
Take independent legal advice before signing any waiver or forbearance.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Coverage on your loan has dropped to 1.15 times against a 1.20 times covenant, tested in three months. You have some cash outside the project. What do you propose to the bank?
selftest.a: Call now with the diagnosis and a revised forecast. Propose a cash cure or partial paydown sized so debt service at the remaining loan meets 1.20 times on current NOI, plus evidence of the fix for the income shortfall (for example a replacement tenant) and extra reporting until it is resolved. Ask for a waiver or amendment for the next test if the fix will land after it. Have your lawyer review any document before signing.

apply: Build an early-warning sheet for a hypothetical loan with four indicators and a trigger level for each that would make you call the bank.

title: Final review: drills and the pass standard
summary: The last review is a set of drills covering the whole course: concept checks, calculations and role-play questions from a sceptical credit officer. The pass standard is to explain the binding constraint on a deal, the lever that fixes it and what that lever costs, without the model open.
body:
You have learned this course when you can answer these drills aloud, with the material closed, in under a minute each. Mr Shabazz, the pass standard is simple to state and hard to meet: name the binding constraint on a deal, the lever that fixes it, and what that lever costs you, without the spreadsheet in front of you.

Question 1. Concept check. Why does a bank care more about certainty of repayment than about your project's profit, and which of the four construction risks is hardest for a first-time developer to close?

Answer. The bank's return is capped at interest and fees while it can lose the whole principal, so it optimises for not losing. For a first-time developer the hardest risk to close is usually completion, because there is no track record. It is closed anyway by renting a track record: an experienced contractor on a fixed or guaranteed-maximum price, an independent cost consultant, a development manager with completed projects, realistic contingency, liquidity outside the project, and a completion guarantee that burns off at completion.

Question 2. Calculation drill. Cost is US$2,000,000 and the loan-to-cost cap is 60 percent. NOI is US$90,000 and annual debt service on the proposed loan is US$70,000. What are the maximum loan by loan-to-cost, the minimum equity, the coverage ratio, and the maximum debt service at a 1.25 times minimum?

Answer. Maximum loan US$1,200,000; minimum equity US$800,000. Coverage US$90,000 divided by US$70,000, about 1.29 times, which passes 1.20 times. At 1.25 times, maximum annual debt service is US$90,000 divided by 1.25, which is US$72,000.

Question 3. Calculation drill. A loan is quoted at 6.0 percent, with a hypothetical 20 percent withholding on interest and a full gross-up. What is the effective cost, and in this course's sizing table, what is coverage at 8 percent with NOI down 10 percent?

Answer. Effective cost is 6.0 divided by 0.80, which is 7.5 percent. In the sizing table, a US$650,000 loan at 8 percent with NOI down 10 percent to US$72,000 gives coverage of about 1.20 times, exactly at the floor: compliant but fragile, with no headroom, so a credit analyst would ask for more equity, a smaller loan, a fixed rate or stronger income evidence.

Question 4. Role-play. "You have never built anything. Why should we lend to you?"

Answer. "You are right that I have no completed development, so I have hired the experience: a contractor that has built this type of building several times, on a guaranteed-maximum-price contract; an independent cost consultant whose budget carries a contingency they support; and a development manager with completed projects. My own cash is spent first and ranks behind you, I hold liquidity outside the project to fund an overrun, and I will offer a completion guarantee that burns off at completion."

Question 5. Role-play. "Your land is in your personal name. Who exactly is the borrower?" And: "If you are 20 percent over budget at month 10, where does the money come from?"

Answer. "The borrower will be a single-purpose company, which will be formed and authorised to borrow, and the land will be transferred into it, or held under the structure my lawyer and tax adviser recommend, before any draw, so you can register a first mortgage. That is a condition precedent I expect to meet by a stated date." On the overrun: "First the contingency, then my liquid reserve outside the project, which I can evidence, under the overrun guarantee. The in-balance test means you would not fund another draw until I had deposited the gap, and my monthly cost-to-complete tracking means I would see it months earlier."

Question 6. The pass standard. State, for a deal of your own invention, its binding constraint, the lever that fixes it and the cost of that lever.

Answer. A model answer, using this course's example at 11 percent: "The binding test is coverage, not loan-to-cost: at 11 percent and 1.20 times, NOI of US$80,000 supports only about US$567,000, against a loan-to-cost cap of US$650,000. The levers are a lower rate, a longer amortisation, higher NOI or more equity. Lengthening amortisation to 30 years adds only about US$16,500 of loan, so the realistic lever is about US$83,000 of extra equity, or a fixed-rate facility near 8 percent, at which loan-to-cost binds again."

Recap of the whole course

A bank sells safety and is structurally cautious. Its decisions are made by a committee reading a memo, through the lens of the five Cs, and limited by capital rules and exposure limits. A construction lender prices completion, lease-up, cash flow and exit, and lends against risk you have already removed. Loans are sized by the lowest of loan-to-cost, loan-to-value and coverage, built on NOI computed the lender's way. The capital stack decides who loses first; only paid-in, subordinated money counts as equity. Security is the second way out and guarantees decide what you personally owe. Abroad, collateral location, withholding and currency hide behind the headline rate. A term sheet is the last cheap moment to negotiate. After closing, report early, test your own covenants and call the bank before a breach.

Four practical habits carry the whole course into real use. Keep a draw schedule and a cost-to-complete tracker, so the in-balance test never surprises you. Keep a stress table of NOI against interest rates, so you always know how close coverage is to its covenant. Keep an all-in comparison table for every lender, so a headline rate never decides alone. And keep a compliance calendar from the day of closing, so reports and tests are met before they are asked for. Each one takes an hour to set up and saves far more than an hour the first time something moves.

Mr Shabazz, keep this final set of drills and repeat it before any real lender conversation. When you can answer every question aloud without notes, you are ready to talk to a credit officer as an equal.
checklist: Bank return capped, loss uncapped: pitch repayment, not profit.
Close completion risk by renting a track record.
Size by the lowest of LTC, LTV and DSCR; work on the binding test.
Count only paid-in, subordinated equity; limit and time-bound guarantees.
Abroad, compare all-in cost and where the risk sits.
Pass standard: binding constraint, its lever, and the lever's cost, without the model.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A credit officer says: 'Your rents come from one market segment. What if demand falls?' Give your answer.
selftest.a: Acknowledge the concentration, then show the numbers: coverage at base and with NOI down 10 and 20 percent, the break-even occupancy, and the lease terms already signed. Explain the mitigation: pre-leases that lock in part of the income, a lease-up and interest reserve, liquidity outside the project to carry the building, a professional property manager with a plan to market to adjacent segments, and a loan sized so coverage stays above the covenant in the downside case.

apply: Have someone read the role-play questions to you as a sceptical credit officer and answer each without notes, timing yourself to under a minute.
